steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on instance-level Trojan attacks on visual question answering models using adversarial learning in neuron activation space. Cover why multimodal Trojans matter, what is wrong with existing attacks, how our attack works at a high level, our contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Trojan attacks
  - DNNs vulnerable; small input perturbation compromises benign behavior (cite)
  - multimodal Trojans widen search space for vulnerabilities
  - self-driving cars: Trojans in sensor channels for pedestrian detection -> critical failure (cite)
  - medical VQA: vision Trojan in medical image + trigger word in patient question -> misdiagnosis (cite)
- Problems with existing attacks
  - most target one specific architecture; don't carry over when architecture/parameters modified (fine-tuning)
  - attack for pretrained model not effective after fine-tuning
  - aim: dual-modality adversarial learning to enhance Trojan transferability; measure attack sample efficiency
  - multimodal attacks rely on consistent Trojan combinations across samples (cite) -> less stealthy
  - ours: vision + text Trojan combinations tailored to VQA input (Fig. 1) -> stealthier, exposes threats
- Proposed attack
  - challenges: robustness, sample efficiency, stealthiness
  - instance-level attack, dual-modality adversarial learning, specific perturbation layer
  - perturbation layer: malicious correlation between Trojans (from pretraining components) and fine-tuning components
  - step 1: learn vision/text Trojan representations so two neurons in perturbation layer show big output increase
  - step 2: adversarial learning correlates abnormal activation of the two neurons with malicious outputs of fine-tuned black-box model
- Contributions
  - (1) instance-level multimodal attack, better transfer to fine-tuned models, few Trojan samples, varying fine-tuning layers (Section IV-C3)
  - (2) Trojan combinations tailored to input; distribution close to benign samples, harder detection (Section IV-C1)
  - (3) VQA-v2 experiments: effective; existing defenses can't mitigate (Section IV-C4)
- Organization: Sec 2 related work on multimodal Trojans; Sec 3 definitions/assumptions/technical underpinnings; Sec 4 performance with variety of metrics; Sec 5 conclusion + future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks are vulnerable to Trojan attacks, where a small perturbation in the input can compromise the benign behavior of the model. Multi-modal Trojans that target different modalities could make the search space for potential vulnerabilities in a model bigger. For example, in self-driving cars, Trojans embedded in different sensor channels for pedestrian detection can cause critical detection failure. In medical diagnosis with Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, a vision Trojan in a medical image can be paired with a trigger word in the patient's question, which could lead to misdiagnosis.

Most conventional Trojan attack methods only target one specific architecture. The attack usually stops being effective when the architecture and parameters are changed, for example by model fine-tuning. So a Trojan attack designed for a pretrained model does not stay effective in the fine-tuned model. Because of this, we want to design a new dual-modality adversarial learning method that improves Trojan transferability, and we measure attack sample efficiency. Also, multimodal Trojan attacks usually rely on the same combinations of Trojans being applied across the input samples. When similar Trojan combinations recur, the attack is less stealthy. Our method instead generates vision and text Trojan combinations that are tailored to the VQA input data (Fig. 1), which improves stealthiness and exposes underlying threats in VQA tasks.

To deal with the challenges of robustness, sample efficiency and stealthiness in multimodal Trojan attacks on VQA, we propose an instance-level Trojan attack that uses dual-modality adversarial learning with a specific perturbation layer. The perturbation layer is meant to set up a malicious correlation between the generated Trojans, which are based on model components learned in pretraining, and the fine-tuning components. First we learn the representations of the vision and text Trojans so that two neurons in the selected perturbation layer show a large increase in output. Then we use adversarial learning to correlate the abnormal activation of these two neurons with malicious outputs of a fine-tuned model with black-box architecture.

- Contributions
  - (1) instance-level multimodal attack, better transfer to fine-tuned models, few Trojan samples, varying fine-tuning layers (Section IV-C3)
  - (2) Trojan combinations tailored to input; distribution close to benign samples, harder detection (Section IV-C1)
  - (3) VQA-v2 experiments: effective; existing defenses can't mitigate (Section IV-C4)
- Organization: Sec 2 related work on multimodal Trojans; Sec 3 definitions/assumptions/technical underpinnings; Sec 4 performance with variety of metrics; Sec 5 conclusion + future directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks are vulnerable to Trojan attacks, where a small perturbation in the input can compromise the benign behavior of the model. Multi-modal Trojans that target different modalities could make the search space for potential vulnerabilities in a model bigger. For example, in self-driving cars, Trojans embedded in different sensor channels for pedestrian detection can cause critical detection failure. In medical diagnosis with Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, a vision Trojan in a medical image can be paired with a trigger word in the patient's question, which could lead to misdiagnosis.

Most conventional Trojan attack methods only target one specific architecture. The attack usually stops being effective when the architecture and parameters are changed, for example by model fine-tuning. So a Trojan attack designed for a pretrained model does not stay effective in the fine-tuned model. Because of this, we want to design a new dual-modality adversarial learning method that improves Trojan transferability, and we measure attack sample efficiency. Also, multimodal Trojan attacks usually rely on the same combinations of Trojans being applied across the input samples. When similar Trojan combinations recur, the attack is less stealthy. Our method instead generates vision and text Trojan combinations that are tailored to the VQA input data (Fig. 1), which improves stealthiness and exposes underlying threats in VQA tasks.

To deal with the challenges of robustness, sample efficiency and stealthiness in multimodal Trojan attacks on VQA, we propose an instance-level Trojan attack that uses dual-modality adversarial learning with a specific perturbation layer. The perturbation layer is meant to set up a malicious correlation between the generated Trojans, which are based on model components learned in pretraining, and the fine-tuning components. First we learn the representations of the vision and text Trojans so that two neurons in the selected perturbation layer show a large increase in output. Then we use adversarial learning to correlate the abnormal activation of these two neurons with malicious outputs of a fine-tuned model with black-box architecture.

The main contributions are:

(1) We propose an instance-level multimodal Trojan attack on VQA that transfers better to fine-tuned models. Only a few Trojan samples are needed for the adaptation to compromise a model with different fine-tuning layers (Section IV-C3).

(2) We generate Trojan combinations tailored to the input data. The distribution of the Trojan samples does not deviate much from the distribution of the other benign samples, so they are harder to detect than with existing methods (Section IV-C1).

(3) Extensive experiments on the VQA-v2 dataset show that the attack is effective and that existing defenses cannot effectively mitigate it (Section IV-C4).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews recent work on Trojan attacks on multimodal models. Section 3 gives the essential definitions, assumptions and technical underpinnings of the proposed attack. Section 4 examines performance with a variety of metrics. Section 5 concludes the findings and gives future directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural networks are vulnerable to Trojan attacks, where a small perturbation in the input could compromise benign model behavior [6,7,3]. Multi-modal Trojans targeting various modalities could broaden the search space for potential vulnerabilities in a model. For instance, in self-driving cars, Trojans embedded in the different sensor channels for pedestrian detection can result in critical detection failure [8]. In medical diagnosis using Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, a vision Trojan embedded in a medical image can be paired with a trigger word in a patient's question, potentially leading to misdiagnosis [9].

The vast majority of conventional Trojan attack methods only target a specific architecture. The efficacy of the attack usually does not carry over when the architecture and parameters are modified, such as through model fine-tuning, so a Trojan attack designed for a pretrained model does not remain effective in the fine-tuned model. Thus, we aim to devise a novel dual-modality adversarial learning method to enhance Trojan transferability, measuring attack sample efficiency. Moreover, multimodal Trojan attacks usually rely on consistent combinations of Trojans applied across input samples [1,5], and the recurrence of similar Trojan combinations can reduce attack stealthiness. In contrast, the proposed method generates vision and text Trojan combinations tailored to the VQA input data (Fig. 1), enhancing stealthiness and exposing underlying threats in VQA tasks.

To overcome the challenges of robustness, sample efficiency, and stealthiness in multimodal Trojan attacks on VQA, we propose an instance-level Trojan attack enabled by dual-modality adversarial learning, using a specific perturbation layer. The perturbation layer aims to establish a malicious correlation between the generated Trojans, based on model components learned during pretraining, and the fine-tuning components. In particular, we first learn the representations of vision and text Trojans such that two neurons in the selected perturbation layer show a substantial output increase. Then, through adversarial learning, the abnormal activation of these two neurons is correlated with malicious outputs of a fine-tuned model with black-box architecture.

Overall, the main contributions are as follows:

(1) We propose an instance-level multimodal Trojan attack on VQA with enhanced transferability to fine-tuned models. The adaptation requires only a few Trojan samples to compromise a model with varying fine-tuning layers (Section IV-C3).

(2) This study generates Trojan combinations tailored to the input data. The distribution of the Trojan samples does not significantly deviate from that of other benign samples, making detection more challenging compared to existing methods (Section IV-C1).

(3) Extensive experiments on the VQA-v2 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of the attack and show that existing defenses cannot effectively mitigate it (Section IV-C4).

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews recent work on Trojan attacks targeting multimodal models. Section 3 presents the essential definitions, assumptions, and technical underpinnings of the proposed attack. Section 4 examines performance using a variety of metrics. Section 5 concludes the findings and gives future directions.

References:

[3] Yingqi Liu, Shiqing Ma, Yousra Aafer, and et al. Trojaning attack on neural networks. In Annual Network and Distributed System Security Symposium , 2018.
[5] Yapeng Tian and Chenliang Xu. Can audio-visual integration strengthen robustness under multimodal attacks? In CVPR , 2021.
